questions.question: How is an HTML document represented as a DOM tree?
questions.title: The DOM tree mental model
questions.direct_answer: The browser represents an HTML document as a tree of node objects rooted at Document. Elements form branches, text becomes text nodes, and APIs expose parent, child, and sibling relationships for reading or changing that structure.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of document, element, and text nodes and their relationships.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming every child node is an element; whitespace in markup can create text nodes.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: The DOM tree is not identical to the render tree, accessibility tree, or the original HTML source.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Document is the root entry point for the page's DOM.
Elements, text, and comments are different node types.
parentNode, childNodes, and sibling properties follow tree relationships.
children skips text nodes; childNodes includes them.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
- An HTML document becomes a logical tree of node objects. The `Document` is the entry point, elements form parent-child branches, and the text inside those elements is represented by separate text nodes. - Relationships in the markup become traversal paths in the API. A list element can expose its parent, its child nodes, its element children, and its previous or next sibling. - For example, `
  • Tea
` creates a `ul` element containing an `li` element, and that `li` contains a text node whose data is “Tea.” Line breaks and indentation between tags can also become text nodes. - That is why `childNodes` and `firstChild` may return whitespace text, while `children` and `firstElementChild` restrict the result to elements. The right API depends on whether text and comment nodes matter to the task. - The DOM is a document model, not a picture of the screen: CSS can hide nodes, pseudo-elements can render without ordinary DOM children, and browser parsing can normalize the source markup.

sections.title: Markup relationships become object relationships
sections.content: Nesting supplies the basic tree shape, but parsing can repair invalid markup and insert implied elements. The resulting DOM is therefore the browser's parsed document, not merely the original source split at angle brackets. Inspecting `nodeType`, `nodeName`, and tree properties reveals what was actually built.

sections.title: Element-only and node-level traversal
sections.content: Element APIs are usually clearer for application UI because they ignore indentation text. Node-level APIs matter to editors, parsers, and tools that must preserve text and comments. A `TreeWalker` or `NodeIterator` can traverse a filtered subtree without custom recursive logic, while ordinary `parentElement`, `children`, and sibling properties are enough for small local moves.

questions.question: How do querySelector(), closest(), and DOM traversal properties differ?
questions.title: Selecting and traversing DOM elements
questions.direct_answer: querySelector() searches downward within a document or element for the first CSS-selector match, closest() checks an element and then walks upward through its ancestors, and traversal properties move one known relationship at a time.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to choose between a subtree query, ancestor lookup, and direct relationship traversal.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Running a document-wide query when the search should be scoped, or using event.target without closest() for nested click targets.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: All single-element lookups can return null, and a selector describes structure rather than guaranteeing the expected element type.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: querySelector() finds the first selector match inside a chosen scope.
querySelectorAll() returns a static NodeList of all matches.
closest() checks the element itself and then its ancestors.
parentElement, children, and sibling properties follow direct relationships.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
- `querySelector`, `closest`, and traversal properties navigate the same DOM tree in different directions. `querySelector()` searches a scope downward for the first element matching a CSS selector, while `closest()` starts at an element and searches upward, including the element itself.

- Direct properties such as `parentElement`, `firstElementChild`, and `nextElementSibling` move one known relationship at a time. They are useful when the component's structure is stable and the required neighbour is already clear.

- For example, a click may land on an icon inside a button. `event.target.closest('[data-action]')` finds the action button, and `toolbar.contains(button)` confirms that the result belongs to the intended toolbar rather than an outer ancestor.

- Queries should be scoped to a stable component root when possible. That reduces accidental matches and documents ownership, although selector cost is rarely the first performance problem on a small page.

- Every lookup can fail after markup changes, so code must handle null and avoid treating a selector match as proof that the element has all expected data.

sections.title: Choose direction before choosing an API
sections.content: A downward search answers “what does this container contain?” An upward search answers “which owning component contains this starting node?” A direct property answers “what is immediately next to this known node?” Framing the relationship first makes the code shorter and less dependent on page-wide selectors.

sections.title: Scope is both clarity and containment
sections.content: Calling `root.querySelector()` limits the search to descendants of root. `closest()` is not automatically limited to that root, so delegated handlers often add `root.contains(match)` before acting. Shadow DOM introduces another boundary: ordinary selectors and closest do not cross a shadow root into a different tree in the same way as light-DOM ancestry.

sections.title: Navigation directions
sections.content:
document or component root
        │ querySelector: search downward
        ▼
     descendant ── nextElementSibling → sibling
        │
        └─ closest: check self, then walk upward → owner
